text:
On the most loving bed
I feel myself dying,
when in nature,
all is as gentle as a garden.


Soft, the white angel's wing
—what pity, what tenderness at last!—
for the first time brushes my shoulders
as a bow brushes a violin.


This freshness of knowing
that we too are leaving here,
what novelty in consciousness,
what soft and subtle persuasion!


What acceptance, what smoothness,
what letting oneself go!
Their edges and points, the acts
round off as they reach me.


Neither the stoic's bloodletting,
who diminished without feeling,
nor the asp that barely kissed
the bud of anxious crimson:


A slow decline, and so sure—
swollen with itself—
that it leaves no room for laments
or fears, nor


even the vague tickle
of that minute to come
in which something that must open
will open before my eyes.


How natural what ends
when it ends by itself!
I go with reason satisfied,
asleep, content, happy.


And I, who lived so many years,
so many years that I lost,
without listening to the sphinx
that whispered beside me!


I did not know that life reclines
and holds itself thus
in that greed of nothingness
which is its divan, its cushion.

translation.title: To Die
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s gentle acceptance of death, including the unfinished “nor” and the final image of nothingness as furniture.
